subject: Census figures, plague mortality, and threshing floor purchase price in David's census narrative

figures.name: Israel fighting men (census result)
figures.note: MT and LXX (Vaticanus) agree on 800,000 for Israel; the Samaritan Pentateuch does not contain 2 Samuel as it is outside the Pentateuch, so SP values are not applicable throughout this passage.

figures.name: Judah fighting men (census result)
figures.note: MT and LXX agree on 500,000 for Judah; note that the parallel in 1 Chronicles 21:5 gives 470,000 for Judah, representing an inter-biblical rather than text-critical divergence.

figures.name: Israel fighting men (1 Chronicles 21:5 parallel)
figures.note: The Chronicles parallel gives 1,100,000 for Israel versus 800,000 in 2 Samuel 24:9, a difference of 300,000 that is an inter-biblical divergence internal to MT rather than a cross-tradition textual divergence.

figures.name: Days of plague offered as divine judgment option
figures.note: MT and LXX agree on 3 days of plague; however, 4QSama from Qumran and the LXX of some manuscript traditions read '3 months' for the second option (flight from enemies), which is also attested differently.

figures.name: Plague mortality (those who died)
figures.note: MT and LXX agree on 70,000 dead from the plague; this figure is consistent across all major text-critical witnesses to this passage.

figures.name: Purchase price of threshing floor (shekels of silver)
figures.note: MT and LXX agree on 50 shekels of silver in 2 Samuel 24:24; the Chronicles parallel (1 Chr 21:25) gives 600 shekels of gold, a major inter-biblical divergence reflecting either different transactions, different metals, or theological elevation of the purchase.

figures.name: Years of famine offered as divine judgment option
figures.note: This is the primary text-critical numerical divergence in 2 Samuel 24: MT reads 7 years of famine while LXX (and 4QSama) reads 3 years, with the Chronicles parallel (1 Chr 21:12) also reading 3 years, giving substantial versional and inner-biblical support for the shorter figure.

systematic_analysis.pattern: Unlike the antediluvian and Shem-to-Abraham genealogies where MT, LXX, and SP diverge systematically by fixed offsets (typically 100 years at first-son birth), 2 Samuel 24 exhibits only one clear cross-traditional numerical divergence: the famine duration (MT 7 years vs. LXX/4QSama 3 years). The remaining figures — census totals, plague mortality, purchase price — show agreement between MT and LXX, with the major numerical tensions being inter-biblical (2 Samuel vs. 1 Chronicles) rather than cross-traditional text-critical divergences. There is no mathematical rule or systematic offset that explains the pattern as a whole; the single famine-duration divergence stands isolated and is best explained by individual manuscript transmission rather than a programmatic editorial policy.
systematic_analysis.pattern_plain: There is really only one number that differs between the ancient Bible versions in this chapter — the length of the threatened famine (7 years in the Hebrew Bible versus 3 years in the Greek translation). The bigger numerical puzzles in this chapter are actually between two books of the same Hebrew Bible (2 Samuel versus 1 Chronicles), not between different ancient versions.

theories.name: Scribal Error / Graphic Confusion
theories.summary: The divergence between 7 years (MT) and 3 years (LXX/4QSama) in 2 Samuel 24:13 may reflect a paleographic confusion between the Hebrew numerals or letters for 7 (שֶׁבַע / zayin) and 3 (שָׁלֹשׁ / gimel/shin), compounded by assimilation to the parallel context of '3 months' and '3 days' in the same verse. The consistent triadic structure of the three offered punishments (3-3-3 or 7-3-3) in different textual traditions suggests a scribe may have harmonized upward (MT) or downward (LXX) toward numerical consistency. Tov's textual analysis of 4QSama supports the view that the shorter reading preserved by the LXX may reflect an early Hebrew Vorlage distinct from the proto-MT tradition.
theories.summary_plain: A copyist may have accidentally changed the number 3 to 7 (or vice versa) in the Hebrew manuscripts, possibly influenced by the fact that the other two punishments in the same verse are both measured in 3 units, or by confusion between similar-looking Hebrew letter-numbers.
supporting_evidence: 4QSama (Dead Sea Scrolls) reads 3 years, aligning with LXX against MT and demonstrating the shorter reading has an independent ancient Hebrew attestation predating the MT standardization.
The parallel text 1 Chronicles 21:12 also reads 3 years of famine, providing strong inner-biblical corroboration for the shorter figure across two independent compositional traditions.
The triadic structure of the three punishments (famine / flight / plague) creating a 3-3-3 pattern has an internal symmetry that makes the 7-year figure look like an expansion disrupting the pattern.

Emanuel Tov's work on the Samuel scrolls from Qumran demonstrates that 4QSama frequently preserves a Hebrew text closer to the LXX Vorlage than to MT, suggesting MT's '7' is a later development in one scribal stream.
Graphic similarity between Hebrew zayin (7) and other numerals, plus the common phenomenon of number-harmonization in scribal transmission, makes simple copying error a plausible mechanism.
weaknesses: Scribal error alone does not explain why MT would systematically differ from both 4QSama and the Chronicles parallel if the variation were random.
The Hebrew words for 7 (sheva) and 3 (shalosh) are not visually similar enough in most scripts to support simple graphic confusion as the primary mechanism.
This theory does not account for the inter-biblical divergences (2 Sam vs. 1 Chr census totals; 50 silver vs. 600 gold shekels) which require separate explanations.

theories.name: Independent Textual Traditions (Two Vorlage Hypothesis)
theories.summary: The most robust text-critical explanation for the 7 vs. 3 year divergence is that the MT and LXX/4QSama reflect genuinely independent Hebrew textual traditions (distinct Vorlagen) that diverged prior to the LXX translation and the Qumran period. The existence of a non-MT Hebrew base text for the Samuel books is well-established through 4QSama, and the consistent agreement of LXX + 4QSama + Chronicles against MT for the famine duration strongly suggests the proto-MT tradition at this point underwent a secondary expansion from 3 to 7, possibly for theological reasons (7 as a number of completeness), rather than the LXX shortening an original 7. This aligns with the broader scholarly consensus (McCarter, Tov, Cross) that the LXX of Samuel often preserves a more original textual form against MT expansions.
theories.summary_plain: The Greek translation and the Dead Sea Scrolls both had access to an ancient Hebrew copy of 2 Samuel that was genuinely different from the Hebrew text that became our standard Bible, and in this case the older copy likely said 3 years while the later standardized Hebrew text was changed to 7 years.
supporting_evidence: P. Kyle McCarter's commentary on 2 Samuel (Anchor Bible, 1984) argues that the LXX of Samuel consistently reflects a superior Hebrew Vorlage preserved also in 4QSama, making independent tradition the default explanation for such divergences.

Frank Moore Cross's work on the local text theory identifies distinct Palestinian, Egyptian, and Babylonian text-types for Samuel, with 4QSama representing the Palestinian tradition that served as the LXX Vorlage.
The triple convergence of LXX + 4QSama + 1 Chronicles on the reading '3 years' provides unusually strong multi-witness support for the shorter figure against MT alone.
The MT tendency toward numerical expansion is documented elsewhere in Samuel (compare MT and LXX figures in 1 Samuel 13:5 for Philistine chariots), establishing a pattern of MT enlargement.

The number 7 carries strong theological and literary significance in Hebrew tradition (completeness, covenant), making it a plausible target for scribal or editorial elevation in the proto-MT tradition.
weaknesses: The local text theory of Cross has been critiqued by scholars including Armin Lange and others who question whether neat geographic text-families can be sustained across all Samuel evidence.
Independent tradition does not in itself explain the mechanism by which the divergence arose — it pushes the question back one level to the origin of the variant within the earlier tradition.
The Chronicles parallel could itself be dependent on a LXX-type Samuel source rather than an independent witness, weakening the apparent triple-witness argument.

theories.name: Theological Motivation (Numerical Symbolism)
theories.summary: A theologically motivated change could explain why the proto-MT tradition elevated 3 years to 7 years of famine: the number 7 in Hebrew scripture carries deep covenantal and completeness symbolism (Leviticus 26 repeatedly invokes sevenfold punishment for covenant violation, and 2 Samuel 21:1 records a 3-year famine for Saul's sin, making a 7-year famine for David's census a theologically weightier punishment). Conversely, the Chronicles parallel may have reduced the figure to 3 years to harmonize with other Davidic famine narratives or to emphasize divine mercy in the immediate withdrawal of the punishment. Theological motivation is difficult to distinguish from independent tradition and may have operated within the scribal process rather than as a competing explanation.
theories.summary_plain: Someone copying or editing the Hebrew text may have changed 3 years to 7 years because 7 is a sacred number in the Bible symbolizing completeness and divine judgment, making the threatened punishment feel more serious and theologically appropriate for David's sin.
supporting_evidence: Leviticus 26:18, 21, 24, 28 invokes sevenfold covenant punishment, making 7 years of famine a natural theological amplification of divine retributive justice in the Deuteronomistic framework.

The number 7 appears in closely related David narratives (7 sons of Saul handed over in 2 Samuel 21:6) suggesting a Deuteronomistic editorial preference for heptadic patterns in sin-punishment cycles.

The Chronicler's theology of immediate retribution (sin → punishment → repentance → relief) is well-documented and could motivate reduction to 3 years to fit the narrative arc where David quickly repents.
The figure 70,000 dead from the plague may have been chosen in deliberate numerical contrast with the census total, and 7 years of famine would echo this heptadic theme across the chapter.
weaknesses: Theological motivation is inherently speculative and difficult to verify because the same numerical symbolism could be invoked to argue for either expansion or reduction.
If theological symbolism drove the change, we would expect more consistent heptadic patterns across the chapter, but only the famine duration shows the divergence.

The presence of 4QSama as an independent Hebrew witness to '3 years' means the theological change, if it occurred, must have happened very early in the proto-MT tradition before the Qumran period, limiting what we can say about the editorial intent.

theories.name: LXX Harmonization to Chronicles
theories.summary: One could argue that the LXX translator (or the LXX Vorlage) harmonized 2 Samuel 24:13 downward from 7 to 3 years in order to align with the 1 Chronicles 21:12 parallel, a well-attested phenomenon in Greek biblical translation where cross-book consistency is imposed. However, this theory is significantly weakened by the 4QSama evidence: since the Dead Sea Scroll fragment also reads 3 years in a Hebrew manuscript predating the LXX's likely influence on Hebrew copying, harmonization of the Hebrew toward the LXX is essentially ruled out for 4QSama, meaning the LXX must have had an independent Hebrew source already reading 3. The direction of dependence almost certainly runs from an original 3-year Hebrew tradition toward the MT's expanded 7, rather than from an original 7 toward LXX harmonization.
theories.summary_plain: It is possible the Greek translators changed 7 to 3 to match the same story in the book of Chronicles, but this theory is largely ruled out because an ancient Hebrew scroll from the Dead Sea also says 3 years, meaning the Greek translators were working from a Hebrew copy that already said 3.
supporting_evidence: Harmonization of parallel texts is a documented LXX translation tendency, particularly in historical books where the translator would have known the Chronicles version.
The number 3 appears in both the famine option and the flight option in Chronicles (21:12), creating pressure toward triadic consistency that a harmonizing translator might impose.
weaknesses: 4QSama reads 3 years in Hebrew, entirely independent of any LXX influence, demolishing the core premise that the shorter reading originated in Greek translation.
The scholarly consensus (Tov, McCarter, Cross) runs decisively against LXX harmonization as the primary explanation for Samuel divergences, favoring instead the superiority of the LXX Vorlage.
If LXX harmonized to Chronicles, we would expect many more numerical alignments between LXX Samuel and Chronicles than are actually attested.
This theory requires the more difficult reading (MT's 7) to be original, but in text criticism the more theologically expansive reading is generally considered secondary.

overall_assessment: The numerical divergences in 2 Samuel 24 are fundamentally different in character from those in the Pentateuchal genealogies: they are not systematic across MT/LXX/SP because the Samaritan Pentateuch has no jurisdiction over Samuel, and the major tensions are inter-biblical (2 Sam vs. 1 Chr) rather than cross-traditional. The one genuine text-critical numerical divergence — 7 years (MT) versus 3 years (LXX, 4QSama, 1 Chronicles) for the threatened famine — is best explained by the independent traditions hypothesis: the proto-MT tradition underwent a secondary numerical expansion from 3 to 7, motivated by theological symbolism of covenantal completeness, while the LXX and 4QSama preserve a more original Hebrew Vorlage reading 3. The convergence of three independent witnesses (Greek translation, Hebrew Qumran scroll, and the Chronicler's parallel) against MT alone constitutes unusually strong evidence that MT's 7 is the deviant rather than the original reading. This passage thus illustrates how the Samuel text-critical problem differs structurally from Pentateuchal chronology: it is a case of localized variant within a multiply-attested tradition rather than systematic editorial policy.
overall_plain: In 2 Samuel 24, the main number that differs between ancient Bible versions is the length of the threatened famine — 7 years in our standard Hebrew Bible but 3 years in the Greek Bible and a Dead Sea Scroll. The most likely explanation is that the standard Hebrew text was changed from 3 to 7 at some point, perhaps because 7 is a sacred number in the Bible, while the Greek and Dead Sea Scroll versions preserved the original. The other big number differences in this chapter (like 800,000 versus 1,100,000 soldiers) are between two books in the same Hebrew Bible rather than between different ancient versions.

bibcrit_assessment.title: 4QSama Decisively Undermines MT Primacy in Famine Duration
bibcrit_assessment.reasoning: The most significant implication of the 2 Samuel 24 numerical divergences for transmission history is methodological: the Dead Sea Scrolls evidence for a pre-MT Hebrew tradition reading 3 years transforms what might have been dismissed as a Greek translator's harmonization into proof of a divergent Hebrew textual stream, validating the Cross-Tov model of multiple ancient Hebrew recensions for Samuel. This means the Masoretic Text, far from being a neutral preserver of the original, underwent at least one numerically significant expansion in the Samuel material, with implications for how we assess MT reliability across the historical books. The passage thus serves as a case study in why text criticism of Samuel must treat 4QSama and the LXX Vorlage as co-equal witnesses rather than secondary corrections.
bibcrit_assessment.plain: A Hebrew scroll found near the Dead Sea says the threatened famine was 3 years, not 7, which proves that the standard Hebrew Bible we use today was changed at some point — this is important because it shows the Greek Bible's translators were not just making things up but were working from real, ancient Hebrew copies that preserved an older reading.

_validation.confidence_note: The core text-critical claims about 2 Samuel 24 are largely sound, but several specific scholarly attributions and a key claim about 4QSamᵃ require verification.

flagged_claims.claim: 4QSama (Dead Sea Scrolls) reads 3 years, aligning with LXX against MT
flagged_claims.reason: The state of 4QSamᵃ at 2 Sam 24:13 needs verification. While 4QSamᵃ often aligns with LXX, the specific reading of '3 years' for the famine in this verse is asserted repeatedly but the manuscript may be fragmentary or lacunose at this point. McCarter and others note LXX reads 3 years, but the 4QSamᵃ attestation specifically for this variant should not be stated as certain fact.

flagged_claims.claim: Frank Moore Cross's work on the local text theory identifies distinct Palestinian, Egyptian, and Babylonian text-types for Samuel, with 4QSama representing the Palestinian tradition that served as the LXX Vorlage
flagged_claims.reason: Cross's local text theory is real, but the precise claim that 4QSamᵃ 'served as the LXX Vorlage' overstates the relationship; Cross argued 4QSamᵃ reflects a text-type close to the LXX Vorlage, not that it was the Vorlage itself.

flagged_claims.claim: compare MT and LXX figures in 1 Samuel 13:5 for Philistine chariots
flagged_claims.reason: 1 Sam 13:5 has a famous textual problem (30,000 chariots in MT), but the LXX reading and whether this is a clear case of 'MT enlargement' vs. corruption is debated; cited as evidence of a pattern, this is somewhat oversimplified.

flagged_claims.claim: 4QSama from Qumran and the LXX of some manuscript traditions read '3 months' for the second option (flight from enemies), which is also attested differently
flagged_claims.reason: This claim is vague ('attested differently') and the specific 4QSamᵃ reading for the flight duration needs verification; the note conflates multiple possible variants without clear documentation.

flagged_claims.claim: P. Kyle McCarter's commentary on 2 Samuel (Anchor Bible, 1984)
flagged_claims.reason: McCarter's II Samuel Anchor Bible volume was published in 1984, which is correct, but the characterization of his argument as making 'independent tradition the default explanation' slightly overstates his more nuanced position.

flagged_claims.claim: The figure 70,000 dead from the plague may have been chosen in deliberate numerical contrast with the census total, and 7 years of famine would echo this heptadic theme
flagged_claims.reason: This is speculative literary-theological reasoning presented as supporting evidence; no scholarly source is cited and the connection is the analyst's inference.

safe_claims: MT reads 7 years of famine while LXX reads 3 years in 2 Samuel 24:13
1 Chronicles 21:12 reads 3 years of famine, agreeing with LXX against MT
1 Chronicles 21:5 gives 1,100,000 for Israel and 470,000 for Judah, differing from 2 Samuel 24:9
1 Chronicles 21:25 records 600 shekels of gold for the threshing floor vs. 50 shekels of silver in 2 Samuel 24:24
MT and LXX agree on 70,000 plague deaths
The Samaritan Pentateuch does not contain 2 Samuel as it is outside the Pentateuch
The number 7 carries symbolic weight of completeness in Hebrew scripture
